One result of that situation is that the men in the gold mining industry have not been able to obtain those increases in wages to which they are entitled and which the management of the mines agree they are entitled to.	.
My hon. friends, as I said, come from the cities and they do not know much about these problems. Their remarks and laughter show that they do not know that in British Columbia two of the gold mines which give employment to a substantial number of men have had to cease operations as a result of the present price of gold and the revaluation of the Canadian dollar which had the effect of reducing the price of gold by $3.50 per ounce. I know my hon. friends would like to laugh that off. I know my hon. friends like to pose as the friends of all workingmen, but when one points out that workingmen are suffering, that men are out of work as a result of government policy, one finds that the socialists laugh.
Not only were two mines in British Columbia closed down and men thrown out of work as a result of this situation; I have a list here of fifty-two other gold mines which had reached the development stage to the extent of sinking shafts, which were ready to extend their operations by continuing mining at new levels, thus giving further employment, but which have suspended underground operations since mid-1946 when the Canadian dollar was revalued and placed on a par with the United States dollar.
I do not suggest, any more than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) suggests, that the whole Canadian economy be drafted to suit the interests of this particular industry even though the welfare of a large number of workers is affected, but I do suggest, and I am glad to find that the minister agreed apparently for the first time last Thursday, that the gold mining industry and the men

whom it employs are entitled to consideration. Their problem, which was created by the restoration of parity in 1946, is a problem which properly concerns the Canadian House of Commons and the Canadian people.
This is not a problem about which hon. members are entitled to take the attitude of saying that other hon. members represent special interests, that they are trying to obtain special advantage or profit to themselves and their friends-

Such conceit and such shallow hypocrisy provide their own answer.
I have given three reasons why we cannot support the continuation of this act without some assurance of steps being taken to free exchange. As I have said, the problem is convertibility and not control, but the continuation of controls under the Foreign Exchange Control Act makes it so easy to avoid grappling with the problem of convertibility. Yet until we have grappled with that problem we shall not be able to remove controls from exchange.
As an example of what is happening as a result of lack of convertibility, one should examine the picture in so far as trade with the sterling area is concerned. In discussing this matter the other day, the minister went at some length into figures which he said showed that our trade had expanded under

the control policy of the government. As a matter of fact, however, the report of the foreign exchange control board shows that our over-all balance of trade with the sterling area in fact declined in 1948 as against 1947.
I should like to read from pages 2 and 3 of the report of the foreign exchange control board, as follows:
Canada's current account surplus with countries other than the United States was $873 million in 1948. Although still very large, this surplus was $347 million smaller than in 1947.
Further down the page there is the following:
This general summary of the main factors affecting Canada's foreign exchange position in 1948 would be incomplete without specific reference to the important and helpful part played by the European recovery program . . .
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of the tremendous volume of dollars and assistance made available under the European recovery program, Canada's balance with the United Kingdom, with the sterling countries, shrank by $347 million in the year 1948. That is a tremendously significant development. It has been referred to in some detail by speakers who have preceded me, and therefore I will not dwell on it. It does mean, however, that we cannot take that rosy assurance from the minister's speech as to the beneficial results of his policies which he would like us to take, because, while we increased our exports to the United States, our flow of trade with the sterling countries has declined by $347 million.
I have here a clipping which indicates to me that we are not the only ones who are concerned with the shrinking of trade in the sterling area. This report appeared in the Montreal Gazette of the 18th of March and concerns a statement made by a Canadian, Mr. Elliott M. Little, member of the executive board of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association in London, England, on March 17. Mr. Little was discussing the question of the shrinkage of trade, and he said to his British audience:
We are not. satisfied that everything possible is being done by you or by ourselves to overcome this dollar problem. It is not only Canada's pulp and paper trade with Britain which has been affected by the exchange problem. In the past year one traditional market after another has been reduced or has disappeared, and old customers for Canadian pulp and paper products have turned to other countries at much higher prices, or have gone without supplies they wished to have.
It is difficult to reconcile oneself to the fact that a country like Australia, with a long tradition of trade with North America, particularly in pulp and paper products, must now buy at inflated prices from Italy, Germany, Finland, and even a little from Japan-all of them recent enemies-and from Sweden, which was neutral, and cannot buy from Canada, a sister dominion and old commercial friend, or from the United States.
Foreign Exchange Control
That is a statement of the facts of the situation under which Canadian trade is now being carried on. On account of the lack of convertibility, countries which previously had been free to trade with one another, and which desire to trade with one another because of their economic and political affinity, can no longer trade. They are forced to buy at higher prices from countries with whom they have nothing in common simply because the currency of those countries is available whereas Canadian dollars are not available to sterling countries, and sterling is increasingly less available to dollar countries. Sterling will be less available to dollar countries if trade between the two shrinks much more; because, if we do not sell to the United Kingdom and to sterling countries and get supplies of sterling, not only will they be unable to buy from us but in the long run we shall be less able to buy from them.
The fourth reason why we cannot support the continuation of this act is its great cost to the Canadian people, not only its cost in terms of trade and what it is doing to lose trade, but the cost of administering it. In answer to a question recently as to the cost to Canada of carrying on her foreign exchange transactions, I received figures showing that the excess of expenditure for gold, United States and other currencies over receipts from those currencies has been $981 million since 1939. That is over $100 million a year for the nine-year period up to 1948. There is only one place which that money can come from and that is out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers. Nearly $100 million a year has had to be raised in taxes from the Canadian people in order to keep the government in the business of foreign exchange where it should not be, certainly not so long as its policies are restrictive rather than making for expansion.
For that fourth reason, because of the tremendous cost to the Canadian people, a cost which we can ill afford to bear with the present rates of taxation, we can not allow this measure to be continued. It would be different if the government showed any signs of really trying to get out of the business of control, but it does not. It restricts our trade, it taxes us to carry on control measures, and it asks for a continuation of this measure for two years without at any time showing any sign of realism, or any willingness to enter into negotiations which would result in the final elimination of these controls which are so expensive, and which so hamper and thwart the Canadian economy.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking again on this bill because, although the debate on this measure has been a good one, we are placed in this

Foreign Exchange Control position, that the government and the house realize the impasse into which we are getting through the inconvertibility of currencies. We are approaching a trade climacteric. We are moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market. Everything has gone well because a market could be found for everything that has been produced. Further, we have been doing well because of the tremendous volume of Marshall-plan offshore purchases made in Canada. We cannot look for a continuation of this sellers' market, nor can we look for a continuation of the great volume of Marshall-plan offshore purchases.
There is a specific danger with regard to wheat. At any moment, wheat may be declared a surplus commodity in the United States. Such a move would cut off approximately $300 million of the annual offshore purchases made in Canada. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this problem of exchange control and convertibility is vitally important. I realize that no one appreciates that more than the minister, and no one appreciates it more than the members of this house. It is because we in this house see the lack of any specific action contemplated by the government that I wish to put forward certain suggestions.
An exchange rate cannot be fixed by edict; it can only be fixed by convertibility into gold at a fixed rate of redemption into gold. A fixed rate without redemption into gold is meaningless. A flexible but convertible rate can only be arrived at through the use of a common denominator and that common denominator has always been gold. There is no evidence to indicate that is not now the case.
We have suggested the freeing of the Canadian dollar. There are certain risks in that course, and they are risks which must be considered. The first risk is: would the Canadian dollar, if exchange control were abandoned, sink to a great discount in the United States? I think, Mr. Speaker, we have evidence that it would not in the operation of what is known as the unofficial market for Canadian dollars in New York. While that unofficial market represents only about five or six per cent of our entire trade, nevertheless it does account for, according to the best figures I could get from New York, between $135 million and $300 million. Mr. Speaker, that is no hole-in-the-wall market. It does give an indication of what would happen to our dollar if controls were removed.
When the parity move was made, the unofficial market was around ten per cent. At one time it went down to a little over 
twelve, but today I believe it is around six and a half per cent and seven per cent. This illustrates what has happened to our dollar on this free market on which our currency is sold in terms of United States dollars. It has improved from twelve per cent to about six per cent in approximately a year's time. This shows that the position of the Canadian dollar, vis-a-vis the United States dollar, is strong. I submit that if we had no foreign exchange control, the dollar would not sell at a great discount, and my evidence is the operation of the unofficial market in Canadian dollars.
The second point which we must consider is: would there be a drain of capital from Canada? Here again our fears are groundless because the history of capital shows that capital has always flowed into a country with a free economy. Capital has always been attracted to a country in which it is given the greatest freedom. The removal of exchange control would be giving capital that freedom. I submit that, far from being a drain on capital, there would be a tremendous increase of capital in Canada.
Furthermore, I submit that this capital, by and large, would be what the minister termed desirable capital. He called it the bricks and mortar capital. I believe it would flow into the development of oil, the development of base metals, the development of our potential iron deposits, and for a dozen and one other purposes for which capital is needed. The situation that obtained in 1929 does not apply today, and I will give you the reason for that at a later stage.
The third question is: would our economy be subject to gambling under pressure of what is known as "hot money"? I submit that is not likely because, first of all, there is very little so-called hot money in Canadian currency outstanding. Our savings accounts, the position of our financial institutions, have never been as strong nor as resilient as they are at the present time. The credit situation is very good. There are no extended loans for security purchases. The exchanges have tightened up the margin requirements and have accomplished a lot of other worth-while things which have made practically impossible speculation and gambling of the type that occurred in 1929. Therefore, I think that the existence of "hot money", the existence of gambling in Canadian funds, is not a risk which we have to run.
Would there be an increase in United States investments in Canada? I think the answer to
that question is obvious. We have shown______
and I think it is a matter of some national pride-that despite the restrictions of the FECB we have had an inflow of capital into

Canada. There was a time immediately after the parity action of 1946 when the movement was very much the other way. But today there are literally billions available for investment in the United States and these billions are looking for adequate employment in the development of natural resources. With the possible exception of Brazil, Canada is the only country left in the world that has a stable government and tremendous untapped natural resources. I think we would have a great increase in United States funds coming into Canada for investment purposes, and those purposes would not be for investment in the stock market. If they want to, the Americans can buy or sell Canadian stocks at the present time, particularly interlisted stocks. As I have said, the restrictive operations of the major stock markets make this sort of speculation much more difficult. The volume and the impact of hot money is now tremendously cushioned. This investment money would not be frightened money. It would be money coming in for long-term purposes.
I want to mention briefly two authorities, both of them British, and what they say with regard to what our present situation is doing to our international trade. The first authority is Sir Stafford Cripps, in an interview which is quoted by The Economist of London of February 26:
He also stressed the difficulties that are being met in expanding British exports to Canada, saying that Britain could not sell all the steel Canada needed because it had to reserve certain quantities of scarce materials for use in bilateral negotiations with other countries.
I skip about eight lines, but I am not taking the statement out of its context at all:
There can be no doubt that the main obstacle to the British export drive to Canada is to be found in the fact that British prices are, by and large, too high for the Canadian market. That fact is likely to be increasingly impressed upon all concerned if the trend of prices in the United States continues to be downward. This disparity in dollar and sterling prices is beginning to call into question the basic effect which the Marshall plan may be having on the relative price and cost structures of Europe and the dollar area. The way in which aid is being applied, and the extent to which the countries of Europe are being encouraged to divert their imports from dollar to non-dollar sources even if the latter are more expensive, is creating a disequilibrium which may call for the most drastic remedial measures, involving exchange adjustments, if the dollar solvency of Marshall Europe is to be restored by 1952.
At the same time, it cannot be said that Canada has chosen the happiest moment from its or Britain's point of view to announce the reimposition of the import duties on British textiles which were suspended in 1947. Overtopping all other issues affecting Anglo-Canadian trade is the possibility of wheat being declared a surplus commodity in the United States, a move which would prohibit the economic co-operation administration from allocating Marshall dollars for offshore purchases of wheat in Canada. If any such misfortune were to happen it would
Foreign Exchange Control face both Canada and Great Britain with a problem the urgency of which would relegate the longer term issues to relative insignificance.
That is from The Economist of last month.
I do not think the seriousness of the problem can possibly be overestimated. I want to quote also from The Banker of London, England, an article by C. Gordon Tether, who has been an adviser to some of the big five banks in Great Britain, and what he has to say on what he calls the Canadian dilemma:
There is general concern at the apparent paradox that in the past year or so the Canadian price level has shown a bigger rise than occurred during the preceding eight years of war finance and post-war adjustment . . . the dominion is beginning to suffer from a money-goods gap of the type familiar in European countries during the past few years . . . To begin with, there is no certainty, even in the short run, that the indirect "Marshall" relief for the dominion's United States dollar position will continue on the present scale beyond the middle of 1949.
Then I skip a paragraph and continue:
Mr. Gardiner, dominion Minister of Agriculture, pointed out in a recent speech that the ban on the use of E.C.A. dollars for "offshore" purchases has already made it impossible for Canadian farmers to sell their linseed, beans and other products, although consumers elsewhere are paying prices fifty per cent above those ruling in Canada.
It would seem, therefore, that Canada must resign herself, even during the currency of the Marshall plan, to the need to resume unrequited exports and, in all probability, to a decline in the amount of convertible exchange she can derive from her favourable trade balance with Europe. The postMarshall prospect is even more disturbing . . . Imports from Canada may be small in relation to total United States production, but resistance to them tends to become intense in times of surplus and falling prices. Canada is therefore liable to find this outlet for her produce blocked just when she most needs it.
It is, in short, unfortunately all too clear that the dominion's external economic prospect is, on a short view no less than on the long, as obscure and as fraught with peril as ever. This being so, the present dilemma of the Canadian government is readily apparent. . . Whatever success attends the drive to obtain permanent markets in the United States, however great the expansion in importsaving production within Canada, markets for the bulk of the dominion's primary produce, readily accessible in bad times as well as in good, will remain in Europe. If those markets are lost, Canada's prosperity will inevitably suffer.
There we have two British authorities who, I think, may be considered to have a sympathetic desire for the mutual well-being of the United Kingdom and of Canada; yet they state in definite and specific terms that under the present situation nothing but a chaotic impasse will happen if convertibility cannot in some way be arranged. That is a pretty serious situation. Because we had record exports in 1948, because we had record purchases by the Marshall plan, because our situation last year was so good, let us not fool ourselves into thinking that we are going to live in this paradise with happy exports for everything we produce, either to the United

Foreign Exchange Control States or to Europe-certainly not Europe. Let us not fool ourselves that we are going to be able to export either our raw materials or our manufactured articles when we see that in terms of barter these countries on a barter economy are willing to pay for the goods that we produce 50 per cent more than they can get them for from us. We cannot sit idly by and say that there is nothing we can do; we cannot sit idly by and say, here is a situation which stumps us. There must be something we can do. There has to be something that we can do. It reminds me of a young officer who was training recruits for the first time on the square. He became frightened and the squad started marching off. The sergeant major said to him: "For God's sake say something, even though it is only good-bye". Our export markets are in that position. I suggest to the government that for God's sake they do something, even though it is only to say good-bye. I am sure that they can do something. I am sure that there are measures which they can take which will at least explore the impossible situation into which we have got ourselves.
The problem is one of convertibility. These European countries have imposed the same sort of restrictions as we have. They have imposed them, as they think, in order to safeguard their own economy. They are neither safeguarding their own economy nor assisting world trade. In fact, they are doing absolutely the reverse.
Of course we cannot go to any other sovereign state and say to it, your laws and your exchange control are bad. We want you to change them. The minister was perfectly right when he said that it would be considered as a gratuitous insult for Canada to suggest to the United Kingdom, or to any other country, that their currency was overvalued or undervalued in terms of the United States dollar. But I do suggest that there is a way in which we can start. The problem is that we have two unknowns, two currencies, and the only way to indicate the relationship of a currency is to relate it to something that is known. It is a sample of what we were taught in school. It is the simple simultaneous equation.
The only known thing to which currencies are eventually related is gold; and I suggest again that in order to obtain this denominator, this relationship, we should allow the operation of a free gold market so that we should get a true relationship of one currency to gold and another currency to gold. By so doing we would be able to obtain a relationship between these currencies, and if they could be converted, one or another, into gold through the operation of the free market, 
surely we would be taking the first step toward convertibility of one currency into another. It is going to be difficult. A great deal of opinion in the United States is against it, but I suggest in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, that they are against it for selfish reasons. Let us see who are opposing it. A most vehement opponent of the operation or the establishment of a free gold market is- and I think he is one authority whom we must consider-a man called Leffingwell. He is the chairman of the board of J. P. Morgan and Company, international bankers. What are the reasons which he gave for opposing the operation of a free market? They were simply these. He said that today the United States dollar is a world currency, and that the United States gold reserves are world gold reserves. If I were the chairman of J. P. Morgan I would take precisely those views, and I would do it for precisely the same reason. If I were a great United States banker I would like to have my dollar and my gold reserves known as the world gold reserve. It would be a tremendous advantage to me. It was the happy position that the pound had at one time, only never in so great a degree. But here the Americans, quite frankly, want to make the United States dollar the only international currency, and the United States gold reserves the world gold reserve. He admitted it.
Let us go a little further. Mr. Walter E. Spahr opposes a free gold market, but he wants the United States dollar to be returned to the gold standard at $35 an ounce. He wishes convertibility of the United States dollar, the one freedom which the United States dollar does not possess at the present time. He wishes it to be restored. In other words, he wishes that you should go to the mint or to Fort Knox with $35 and buy an ounce of gold. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if that were done, even with the tremendous reserves of gold today, Gresham's law would become effective immediately, and there would be a run on the gold reserves of the United States.
We like to think that the United States currency, in regard to gold, is in a happy position. So it is; but let us remember that there are $141 billion worth of United States government obligations outstanding, and these obligations are a prime responsibility of the United States government. There are two other authorities, the economists national committee and the New York board of trade. They have opposed the operation of a free gold market, and have opposed it for these reasons. Therefore unquestionably we would meet great opposition. Not only that, but we

would meet opposition from the United States treasury and the international monetary fund.
I suppose, however, there is a great and growing body of opinion that this is the only method by which we can obtain a norm by which currency can be judged. And unless some norm is found, some agent of convertibility, bilateralism and restraint of trade through monetary restrictions are going to be increased and intensified. We Canadians, because of our erstwhile happy position between the United States and Great Britain, are going to find that we are the supreme sufferers in this impossible situation; and instead of being, as I believe, the greatest per capita exporter, we shall find ourselves in a position in which we cannot export.
Immediately a surplus is built up in the United States, immediately they have a surplus of manufactured goods and of wheat, where are we going to sell our wheat? Where are we going to sell our surplus goods? Immediately that happens we are going to be in an impossible position.
I suggest that certain action should be taken.
I am sure the permanent officers of the international monetary fund are as perturbed as any of us about this situation. I have no doubt they are as anxious as we are to find some method of convertibility. The whole reason for the international monetary fund, the whole hopeful theory behind Bretton Woods, was to prevent the international banditry of jockeying with currencies, and doing all the things which shocked Europe and the world in the late twenties and all through the thirties. Had it worked, possibly no one in the world would have condemned it. It has developed however an entirely new sort of international banditry, the international banditry of bilateralism. That is, two countries get together and one says, "We will sell you this commodity at an entirely fictitious price, in terms of a paper currency. We will sell it to you, not in terms of currency but in terms of something else which you sell us at a far higher price than it would bring in terms of international currency." They price themselves out of the world market.
That is the international banditry that is going on today, and it is a type of trade banditry and unrest which we cannot stand. Until some method is found to overcome this impossible position, we are going to suffer- and to suffer most acutely.
I suggest we should go immediately to the international monetary fund and ask for a plenary session. We would make our claim as one of the great suppliers of food, one of the great creditor nations in terms of foodstuffs, metals and materials required in world recovery. On a per capita basis we are probably the greatest supplier of those
Foreign Exchange Control materials, whether they be food, metals or anything else.
I suggest we should go to the international monetary fund, ask for that plenary session, and put our case on the table before all the countries, saying, "We do not want to take unilateral action in this matter. But unless, through the agency of this fund, we can obtain convertibility of exchange, not at the behest and requests of the national treasuries of the various countries at the pegged rates, but at free rates and rates in terms of gold, our exports are liable to be cut off, and our import position becomes impossible because the countries have priced themselves out of our markets. Therefore our export trade upon which, more than any other country in the world, we depend, is being destroyed. If our export trade is destroyed, our national sovereignty is threatened, because our economy is so desperately bound up with that export trade."
I say that unless we can get some agreement with the other nations of the fund we must be prepared to protect ourselves by unilateral action and enter into what I believe to be the unfortunate business of barter. Even though it was mentioned by the foreign exchange control board, I consider it a retrograde step. But we should strain our efforts first toward obtaining convertibility of currencies through the operation of the free gold market.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot well understand why some hon. members who supported the Bretton Woods agreement now take the stand which some on this side of the house have taken. I am one who believes that we must look into the cause and effect of all the trouble we have got into. I am not one of those who criticize the ministers of the crown because I think they are doing their best under a very heavy burden. I have always tried to show ordinary Christian charity toward my political opponents of all kinds. I have always tried to get on with people. Mind you, some of them are hard to get on with, but I get on with them anyway. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has been carrying a heavy burden, both as assistant to the former respected Minister of Finance and in connection with his other duties. He has worked very hard.
I was one of those on this side of the house who opposed the principles of Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks because I realized the trouble into which the government would be led. I know I was right at that time. So far as Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks are concerned, they got us into this trouble. A great mistake was made by hon. members on this side of the house in agreeing to that, although I was the exception. The govern-

Foreign Exchange Control ment have been driven into making mistakes along that line.
I am going to speak for only a few minutes; I was down to follow the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). When I opposed Dumbarton Oaks and Bretton Woods I did it for many reasons. I did not like the international monetary fund and international bank features of the agreements; which have had a great effect upon the bill now before the house. They led us into our present imbroglio. I was against the international bank and the international fund which are the basis for the present exchange control bill. I did not believe in the international monetary fund at that time. I said that some pay in and some do not, that some take out and some do not. I referred to the man who broke the bank at Monte Carlo. Tennyson said about this particular matter:
Our little systems have their day;
They have their day and cease to be;
They are but broken lights of thee,
And thou, O Lord, art more than they.
That is what he said in "In Memoriam". Public finance is different from private finance, and when I have completed the few remarks I want to make in this connection I shall have said what I want to say on the motion. I have had some experience with public finance in connection with city government and I know some of the mistakes that can be made. I was a member of the treasury board from 1909 to 1914. In 1915, the second year of the war, we called for quotations, like the present Minister of Finance, from some of the chartered banks, for a loan of $8 million or $9 million on treasury notes signed by the mayor and treasurer of the city. We received quotations of four and a half, four and three-quarters, four and seven-eighths and five for those treasury notes.
I decided to telephone Chicago and New York and I was able to obtain a loan of $9 million from the Chase and National City banks at one and a half, one and a quarter and one and three-quarters. On January 5, 1915, we had $28 million of a sinking fund with which to pay that debt. I suggested to the legislature that there should be an amendment in the city act to permit the city to use that sinking fund for the payment of treasury notes at the current rates.
After that it was decided that instead of the various civic boards handling their own sales of bonds, boards such as the Toronto harbour board and the transportation board and so on, the city would handle everything. At that time there was not a public utility paying its own way. I brought in the late Thomas Bradshaw to act as finance commissioner and from then on we had public TMr. Church.]
discussions of the estimates at open board meetings. A pay-as-you-go system was adopted and there was no inflation of revenues but there was a reduction in the tax rate. In 1915, 1916 and 1917 the expenditures totaled $8 million.
In 1916 I advised the city to apply for legislation to substitute serial bonds for sinking fund bonds and the result was that we were able to refund all our securities and pay something off each year. This was a blessing to civic finances in that we were able to secure loans for debentures at the highest possible rates of any other municipality in the province.
In conclusion I want to say that I was one of those who opposed Dumbarton Oaks and Bretton Woods. We on this side of the house are just as much to blame as the government for the mistakes that have been made. I am willing to admit that. There are also the Geneva and Havana agreements. I was the only one on this side of the house who objected. We should have told our friends in Washington that preferential trade is a family matter and beyond discussion outside the empire.
I am glad I took the stand I did with regard to Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks because they proved to be wrong. They have destroyed preferential trade and they have made us dependent on Washington for many things. They have placed us beyond hope. I am glad I was the only Conservative on these benches who opposed those notorious agreements which have ruined Canada and brought us to disaster. We cannot blame the government entirely for we on this side of the house are just as much to blame. My hon. friends to the left, except those to my far left in the corner, were in exactly the same boat.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words against the extension of this act and will have to disagree with the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). The premium on United States currency was a great help to all farmers, lumbermen, fishermen and exporters of goods in the maritime provinces. The member for Charlotte went back to 1918 and 1919 and said that the banks paid a different rate on United States currency at that time. They paid a different rate, but it never varied over one per cent in all that time. He said that the Americans came over, put their currency in the bank and received the premium, and that the fishermen received no advantage. That is not correct because when the American buyers put their currency in the bank and received the premium they had to pay out the premium to the fishermen, lumbermen, pulpwood sellers and farmers.

During the years 1918 and 1919 I shipped hundreds of cars of potatoes to the United States and Cuba, and for every one of those carloads I paid the farmer from $100 to $300 per car more than I received for them in United States funds. But everyone made a good profit that year. That shows that the premium was a blessing to our farmers, fishermen and lumbermen of the maritime provinces, and of all Canada, the gold miner and everyone else. It was a great mistake when the Canadian dollar was raised to parity.
The member for Charlotte said that he sold fish and received Canadian currency for it in accordance with the foreign exchange control order of 1939. That order reads:
No person shall, without a licence from the board, accept payment in Canadian dollars for any property exported, or to be exported, to the United States.
Therefore if he sold fish for export to the United States it was contrary to the act.
As I said before, the 10 per cent premium was a great blessing to the farmers, fishermen and lumbermen of the maritime provinces, and of all Canada. It brought more United States dollars into Canada than the austerity program has. We would have plenty of United States dollars today if we had only retained the premium.
The Liberal policy has always been free trade. On November 17 over the radio they put embargoes against United States goods. They did not increase the duty; they placed an embargo against United States goods. That was a great detriment to our export trade. The premium increased our export trade; the premium brought millions of dollars into Canada by way of investment. Now the foreigner is scared to bring his money into Canada because he is afraid that he will never get it back again. The government is today allowing the manufacturers of Canada hundreds of thousands of dollars of United States currency to send over to the United States and other countries to buy potato starch and cornstarch to bring into Canada. At the same time the government is buying in the maritime provinces potatoes which they will dump. Those potatoes should be put into starch to take the place of the starch they are importing, and for which they are using United States currency. The imported starch is in competition with our own starch and is driving the price of our own starch down to the extent of hundreds of dollars per carload. This spring we will be dumping potatoes in the maritime provinces because of the bringing in of corn and potato starch.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause one carry?

There is just one matter I should like to take up with the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, and that is the enforcement of these regulations. During the past year and a half a number of complaints have been made to me about the enforcement of these regulations and the failure of the officials to respect the spirit rather than the letter of the law. I want to make it immediately clear that what I am about to say is not a criticism of the customs officers connected with the enforcement of this legislation. They have the regulations and they have to go by them. I would be the last person to make uncalled for allegations of injustice against customs officers in the administration of these regulations, for personal reasons.
I suppose I have to explain that statement. It is simply this, that for years my father was in the customs service and I know something of the work in connection with enforcement. What I wish to bring to the attention of the committee, and the minister particularly, is this. In the application of this legislation care should be taken to see that it is administered with discretion and with the avowed purpose of preventing anything of an unjust or tyrannical nature.
I realize that some found contravening these regulations will raise the defence that they were unacquainted with the regulations. That defence, of itself, should not be sufficient to

Foreign Exchange Control guarantee the return to them of the moneys forfeited to the crown. Recently I was in one of the maritime provinces and was informed that on a number of occasions refunds of such moneys were made.
I am going to bring to the attention of the committee two cases that I brought before the foreign exchange control board, as examples of cases where refunds were improperly denied. In the one case, a resident of the province of Saskatchewan was crossing the line at Windsor. When he came to the line he was asked if he had any United States money in his possession. He said "Yes, I have $86 in my possession". He was then asked if he had the necessary travel permit and he said, in effect, "No, I have not. I endeavoured to deposit this money before coming here, but this is a holiday and I have not been able to do so. I am not concealing it in any way". The order was made that the money be forfeited, the wording of the order being as follows:
that the currency so seized shall remain forfeited in view of and on your failure to declare and offer same for sale to an authorized dealer of the board as required by section 22 of the Foreign Exchange Control Act.
There was no concealment. There was an immediate answer to the questions asked. That this man was in no way deceptive in his answers was admitted by the control board when application was made for the return of the money. I personally communicated with the control board, and I shall read in part from the answer I received.
When leaving Canada at Windsor in July, Mr. Boruff, when questioned by a customs officer, declared having $86 in U.S. currency in his possession but was not in possession of the necessary travel permit and $76 was accordingly seized under the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Control Act. The reason for the seizure was not because of any attempt to conceal from the customs officer that he was carrying the currency but because of his illegal possession of it.
I think that is going too far, sir. There was no concealment, not even an endeavour to conceal. As soon as he was approached by the customs officer, he gave him the facts. In my opinion, that is a tyrannical exercise of discretion on the part of the board in refusing to permit this man to have his money. He established his bona tides and his honesty, which was admitted by the board, and it was tyrannical for them to continue to uphold the order of forfeiture.

The money was never
returned?
It was not returned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know how long this man had had the $86 in his possession?
I cannot give the minister that information. No question of that kind was raised by the foreign exchange control board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I trust my friend appreciates the reason for my question. Anyone who has more than $10 in United States currency is supposed to turn it in.

I realize that. It was a matter of a few days prior to the date in question, when he crossed the line, that he obtained this money.
The next case I should like to mention, and I mention these cases because they illustrate a lack of the exercise of proper discretion on the part of the board, is a case from my constituency. A man received word that a relative had died in Minnesota. The word was received on a Saturday in a small town in Saskatchewan. He obtained a few United States dollars so that he could cross the line to attend the funeral on the Monday. He crossed the line on Sunday and admitted that he possessed $22 in United States funds. Forfeiture of the money was ordered and that order was upheld by the foreign exchange control board.
It is that type of thing, sir, that arouses people to a realization of the injustice that follows bureaucratic interpretation of the law by the board. Parliament does not want to place honest Canadians in a position of having their money forfeited under circumstances such as those. If there were an appeal to the courts, sir, and the appeal were not from the hired man to the hired man's employer, persons such as those I have mentioned would be assured of justice. There being no appeal to the courts, I make an appeal to the minister.
I ask him whether, in his opinion, it was ever intended that this emergency legislation should be used in a manner that can only have the effect of diminishing the respect for law in the minds of the people and increasing their contempt for bureaucratic power thus exercised and above the law. Parliament is asked to place emergency powers in the hands of this board, and above the courts. Certainly, sir, my opinion is, and I think I am expressing the viewpoint of members in all parts of this house, that the board should endeavour at all times to exercise its discretion for the benefit of the citizen when that citizen has clearly shown the absence of any intent to defraud, defeat or in any way hinder the administration of this legislation.
The minister who is in charge of the administration of these regulations should be in a position to assure parliament that harsh, rigorous, unbending and tyrannical interpretation of these regulations will be reduced to the minimum.

I know that there have been occasions when members of the house have felt that my stand on behalf of the need of preserving appeals to the courts has been advanced to too great an extent. I make no apologies for taking that stand. Following criticism that those who administer this legislation were being placed above the law, finally a year ago provision was made to enable a person who was illegally dealt with or tyrannically treated to take proceedings in the courts. But action is made subject to one condition. No matter what his damage, no matter what his loss, no matter how unjust the conduct of the official might be, the person who is wronged is restricted to nominal damages, which means one dollar, but with no costs of action. The only satisfaction that a law-abiding Canadian citizen has, if he takes proceedings, is that if he is the first he may find his name in the law reports. In return for being perpetuated in that way, he is obliged to submit himself to payment of the costs of action and is denied damages.
Now when this legislation is being reconsidered, provision should be made to assure to the individual who is wronged the right that Canadians should have as against officers of the state who act beyond the powers of the legislation under which they purport to act: a right of action without the necessity of leave for a petition of right being granted by the crown.
In Great Britain there are many such bureaucratic regulations and orders. I think there are ten thousand different cases in which an individual may be searched without a search warrant, under legislation now in effect. But the individual has certain rights which are denied under this legislation. Where he is wronged, he may take proceedings in the court without being required to secure the permission or the consent of the crown. I think that we in this parliament, now that we have accepted the principle of this legislation, should make it a point to do three things. First, we should assure that the law be administered with equality to all. Second, we should assure that no one shall be penalized who, through innocence or ignorance, has committed a contravention of the legislation. Finally, we should insist on the preservation for the individual of right of action against the crown; providing that the crown, in the event of its officials acting illegally, in administering this act, shall be liable for damages to the extent of the damage sustained by the citizen.

I wish to draw your attention briefly to what this government, especially the Department of Trade and Commerce under the clever direction of its present minister, has done to relieve the situation created last year in eastern Quebec and the maritimes owing to the lack of European markets for our lumber production.

Although officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce, in both Ottawa and London, have assisted in the complicated negotiations, it is true that the maritimes and eastern Quebec lumber industry deserve much credit for having successfully developed this business.
We have just been informed of contracts with the United Kingdom and Ireland which will considerably aid our lumber industry of eastern Canada. The details of some of these contracts are as follows: Of Eastern Canadian spruce: the original requirement by the British timber control was 90 million feet, 30 million feet more than purchased in 1948.
It is my information that 80 million feet has been placed, and that additional contracts are being negotiated which, if successfully concluded, will bring the total volume for shipment in 1949 up to approximately 125 million feet instead of the 90 million originally indicated. Pit props: the United Kingdom has contracted for approximately 225,000 cords of pit props for her mines.

Oh, oh.

These pit props are produced mostly from spruce and jack pine, and shipments are made from the maritime provinces and Quebec. The value of these contracts amounts to approximately five and a half million dollars.
Hardwood: I have also been informed that the United Kingdom is expected to purchase approximately 10 million feet of hardwood lumber from eastern Canada. This contract is, however, yet to be confirmed.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I thank the Minister of Trade and Commerce for having so effectively given his best attention to my representations and to the representations made by members of our sister provinces to the east. Our lumber producers, and all those who make a living in our lumber industry, will receive the news of these new contracts with great relief and satisfaction.
The Progressive Conservatives may shout their opposition to their heart's content; they will not prevent the public from appreciating the good effects of our policy, which has proven to be in the best interest of the Canadian people.

Now that my hon. friend has raced through his remarks I wonder whether I can get an answer from the minister. I should also like to ask this question. How many seizures of money took place in 1947 and 1948 by provinces, and in how many cases were the seizures released and the money returned to the applicants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I completely agree with the point made by my hon. friend in his initial remarks that officials of' the board, or the customs officers who act for them, should in no case be harsh and tyrannical, as he put it. I suppose that all of us who are members of parliament have had some of these cases

brought to our attention. I know that I have had them and I have taken them up with the board. I do not think that the actions that have been brought to my attention have been harsh or tyrannical. I am free to confess that in some cases it seemed to me that the customs officers might have used a little more discretion and given the person the benefit of the doubt as to his bona fides. However, no one will realize better than my hon. friend the difficulty of giving wide discretionary powers in cases of this kind because it is so easy to play favourites. If there is a breach of the law, in the absence of very special extenuating circumstances, certain conclusions must flow. However, I do not differ with him, or with other hon. members with whom I have discussed this question, that judgment should be exercised by people who are in charge of enforcing these regulations, but favouritism should not be shown.
As to the number of seizures, I have not the breakdown by provinces, but I have them for the country as a whole. I shall give the seizures in total, and perhaps I can obtain the breakdown later. In 1947, 347 seizures were maintained and 321 released. The seizures maintained involved a total of 10,991 United States dollars. The seizures released involved 17,807 United States dollars. These are seizures of $100 and under. In 1948, the number of seizures maintained amounted to 1,501, involving 30,768 United States dollars, and 13,668 Canadian dollars. The seizures released in 1948 amounted to 975, totalling 27,003 United States dollars and 1,770 Canadian dollars. At the end of 1948 there were 228 seizures still pending, involving 5,961 United States dollars and 1,768 Canadian dollars.
Only one case was referred to a court for final decision in 1947. In 1948 there were five cases referred to the courts. Seizure was maintained in three and the board's decision was reversed in the other two. I shall try to get the breakdown by provinces.

The minister says that he agrees the action of the officials should not be tyrannical. Does he not also agree that, in circumstances such as those that I referred to him, the facts were such that the exchange board, in the exercise of its discretion, and having regard to the rights of the individual, might have released the moneys held, since in both cases there was no intent nor was any subterfuge perpetrated with a view to undermining the law? I feel, sir, that these two cases were proper ones for consideration.
The minister has not answered the question that I asked him as to whether or not
Foreign Exchange Control he thinks the time has come, in the granting of these extraordinary powers, that any individual wronged by the illegal exercise of powers by any of the officials, or by the usurpation of powers by them in the discharge of their duties, should have a right of action against such officials and not be limited to the sum of one dollar as nominal damages, irrespective of the enormity of the offence and the interference with his rights and the damage suffered by him. .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the first point my hon. friend has made quite an appealing case, as he has presented it. My own experience has been-and similar cases have been brought to my attention by my own constituents and others-that there is nearly always some difference of opinion, or some conflict between the statement of facts put forward by the person who is complaining and the report we get from the customs officers.
I was quoting from the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is sometimes difficult to judge as between the two conflicting stories.
The hon. member raises the point that there should be some recourse against the public officers in the performance of their duties. I do not think I can agree with that. My understanding is that in the Customs Act and the Excise Act for years there have been provisions analogous to that contained in the Foreign Exchange Control Act, protecting officers in the performance of their duties from being exposed to actions for damages. I was informed at the time the act was brought in that the provisions put in the Foreign Exchange Control Act were, with of course the appropriate changes, identical in their terms with those in the Customs Act and the Excise Act and other revenue acts for ^ears.
I should not think there would be any special reason for removing that protection from customs officers exercising their functions in this instance, or that it should be any different from the protection they are afforded in exercising their duties as customs officers proper.

I have another point I should like to bring up-this is not the first time I have mentioned foreign exchange to the minister. We are really dealing with an act known as the Foreign Exchange Control Act. And I might say to you, sir, that I think a lot of this difficulty rests with the minister -and I am sincere about that.
There was an error in judgment on the minister's part, and I am going to point it out. I will point it out now, because I think there should not be any recurrence of it.
1722	HOUSE OF
Foreign Exchange Control I know that we have complaints where constituents are dealt with unjustly, and they do not receive the compensation due to them.
I think it is the duty of a member to bring this to the minister's attention, because the fault lies with him.
He carried out the same, perhaps I should not use the word tactics, when he was minister of militia. It was most difficult to get the present minister to bring down legislation in the house. I remember that one time when he was minister of militia he made a speech which should have been made here in the House of Commons. We asked him about that speech the same afternoon and in a jocular way he said that it was a political speech, and that we would not wish to hear a political speech. Having said that, he was not very serious about it.
That happened on Friday, May 23, 1947.
I hold in my hand an amendment to the Foreign Exchange Control Act, as it is set out in P.C. 2045, and it is that issue I wish to take up this evening. What happened on that afternoon? The house was in session at that time. I might say that the amending order in council was here. I say the minister should have come to the house, as has been done many times by ministers of the crown, and should have informed the house of the amendment. He should have given us the same information as to the amendment. But instead of that he went on the air at night.
We have a press gallery up here, and they could have given the country the information, but the minister thought better to give it out as a broadcast. What happened? The public did not know anything about it.- And that was the condition in May, 1947.
The months of May, June and July passed. Then what happened? Enforcement officers were appointed. I say that the administration is wrong and that the minister* was wrong. First we have the Minister of Finance dealing with the Foreign Exchange Control Act, and then the administration comes through the Minister of National Revenue.
Two citizens . in my constituency were picked up by officers at the international bridge at Lansdowne in 1947. Naturally I wrote to the minister responsible, in that instance the Minister of National Revenue. He washed his hands of it, and said that this was a matter for the foreign exchange control board.
I immediately brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Well,
I did not get very much information there, except to find out who was carrying out the enforcement. What did I find? In the course of a short time in the following session the minister placed hundreds of these enforce-


ment officers all across Canada. These were not trained. And I should like to place myself on record as saying that if this had been left in the hands of the inland revenue branch I believe all of these people would have been justly dealt with. I say that because the enforcement officers with the inland revenue branch are well established officials who have chosen that branch of the service for their life's work. Many of them are returned soldiers, and veterans of the first world war. They know how to deal with these infractions.
However, as soon as the apprehension is made these people are passed on to Ottawa, with the result that the work of the enforcement officers here overlaps. First there is the Minister of Finance, then the foreign exchange control board, and then the Minister of National Revenue.
I am now going to ask my question. What happened? A form was sent out by an enforcement officer over here in the foreign exchange control board. I would like to know who Mr. C. A. Rowe is. This officer was appointed on June 2, 1947. Then, who is J. E. Rowe, appointed on September 22, 1947?
In order to obtain the information I wanted I had to ask these questions:
1.	How many enforcement officers are employed by the foreign exchange control board?
2.	Who are they?
3.	What date were they appointed?
4.	Where are they located?
5.	What salary does each receive?
Naturally one would think that an official who is acting as part of a government organization would be recorded. I wanted to know if this was an honorary appointment. So what did I find? The answer was:
As the officers provided to the board are employees of the Bank of Canada, their salaries are not a matter of government record.
Here we have this document signed by C. A. Rowe. At that time the present Secretary of State for External Affairs was his chief. I did not know that; perhaps I should have directed my question to him.
This is where the administration is wrong. This letter was sent out, and let me point out where it is not quite fair. It is dated September 5, 1947, and, refers to the minister's statement:
In his statement of May 6. 1947, which was given wide publicity in the daily newspapers and over the radio the Minister of Finance announced that customs officials would be instructed to enforce the new permit regulations strictly and that prosecutions would be instituted in cases where Canadians have unlawfully accumulated United States funds or have attempted to export them without permit.
That letter was sent out on September 5, 1947. It was more or less protecting the

minister, and intimated that he had done the proper thing. I can only say again that the Minister of Finance did not do the proper thing.
I am sorry the Prime Minister is not here tonight, but even in his absence there is a recommendation I should like to make. It took me all last year to get this return of 168 pages. No one can tell me that an injustice has not been done. According to the figures given to the hon. member for Lake Centre a moment ago, in 1947 there were 347 cases, the collections were $10,991. This was retained. But they returned $17,000 in 321 cases. I have every one of those names on the list, and not many of them exceeded $50. That money should be returned on the ground that the minister erred in his judgment.
I say that because in December 1947, when Bill No. 3 was before the house, he saw his mistake. Why did he see it? Because he knew then what had happened. In January of 1948 he saw fit to advertise in newspapers across Canada. This is what he should have done the morning after he went on the air on May 26, 1947. The minister will find the details of the Renaud case on file. I do not know why he did not return the money. That woman was just as innocent as she could be. Can the minister tell me why the money was not returned? After he answers that, I should like to put another question. Can you answer my question first?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why does not my hon. friend address the Chair?
It is all right, I will address the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member was a
Speaker in a legislature for years.

I want to ask the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, why he has not returned this money. There is another case that I read of only yesterday in the Financial Times. This case was not correctly stated by the foreign exchange control board. This man is a French Canadian, Mr. Peter Brunet, and when he was crossing the bridge en route to Ormstown, Quebec, the English-speaking officer asked him-he works in my constituency-what money he had. He told them he had $5. He thought they were asking him about United States money. They asked for his purse, and when he gave it to them they found $68 Canadian funds in it. They took $43 from him. That man was innocent.
That is why I find fault with the administration of the act. If we had the old trusted inland revenue men they would have told the man to leave the money there because they would know he was coming back on Monday morning. But what was done? These other
Foreign Exchange Control officers put it in an envelope and sent it behind the iron curtain to the foreign exchange control board. The man was penalized and the money has not been returned. The minister knows both these cases and I am glad of this opportunity to bring them before him again. Will the minister state why these moneys have not been returned to Miss Renaud and Mr. Brunet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The details of these particular cases have gone out of my head at the moment. Many of these cases are brought to my attention, but I do recall my hon. friend took up with me these two particular cases. From the reports which I got from the officials of the board I came to the conclusion that there was no greater justification in these two cases for returning the money than there would be in several hundred others, and consequently the money was not returned.
Who is Mr. Rowe and how long has he been appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that I cannot give an answer offhand, although I can get the information. I cannot keep track of hundreds of employees in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have only been in the chamber a few minutes because I do not believe in sitting at seven-thirty. I think it is a lot of nonsense because no one is here. I heard what the hon. member for Lake Centre had to say and I agree with everything he said because he talks common sense. But I cannot go as far with the last speaker. If we are going to talk about each individual case involving $10 here and $10 there the bill will never get through. There are one or two ways in which I do not approve of the foreign exchange control. I do not know much about foreign or any other kind of exchange because I have never had any money except what I could borrow.
The other day the Minister of Agriculture said that he always spoke as a politician. I do not, because I do not know anything about politics. My riding borders on the United States and many of my people have to cross the line. There are one or two instances that I want to bring to the attention of the minister. Some of us in British Columbia are honest; we do not all come from the mari-times.
Those are the ones from Saskatchewan.

We are allowed $150
United States to cross the line. We may cross the line and being conservative, in the economic rather than the political sense, we save our money and bring back $75. Being honest people in British Columbia, particu-

Foreign Exchange Control larly in the Fraser valley, we turn in $75. Then when we want to go across the line later in the year we cannot get any money. The minister knows that that is the fact. We are not complaining about being allowed only $150 a year, but when we bring back $75-I never do because I happen to be married-we should be given credit. Unlike the Minister of Agriculture, I am not a politician but my riding borders on the United States and these regulations affect my constituents most unfairly.
An act was passed in 1946 permitting a person to have $100 United States currency in his possession; is that still in effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is $10.
When was the act amended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not remember the exact date, but I think it was the date referred to by the hon. member for Kingston City. I do not want to interrupt, but I indicated before dinner that unfortunately I can be here only for a short time this evening. I gather that the committee wants to discuss this measure for some considerable time. If we could finish in ten or fifteen minutes I could stay, but if not I should like to adjourn the debate and have the house go on to something else.

I shall not be long as I am not going to go into details of cases, but there are one or two things I should like to say with regard to the administration of the Foreign Exchange Control Act.
I think there is on the part of the foreign exchange control board far too much of an attitude of distrust toward people in business. I am perfectly satisfied from what I have seen that there is too great a readiness to prosecute. There are many transactions where the regulations have been technically broken but where there has not been the slightest intent on the part of the individual involved to commit an infraction. I feel that there is far too great readiness to distrust the people involved instead of a willingness to sit down with them to discuss the problem.
In connection with the second aspect of the matter that I should like to discuss, I offer this illustration. This particular case involved a substantial amount and it actually resulted in the saving of considerable United States exchange. But the officers of the board considered there had been an infraction. I am satisfied that if there had been one it was purely a technical one. The officers and accountants and auditors of the board went into this place of business in Toronto and asked to see their books and vouchers. The head of the business readily agreed. He said: "You may make yourselves comfortable here. iMr. Cruickshank.]
We will produce anything you want to see." The officers were not satisfied. They said: "We would like to take your books away. Have you any objection?" He said: "Certainly I have objection. You can take copies of anything you want. You can photostat anything that is here, but I am not going to have my books taken out of my place of business." They were not satisfied with that. Nothing was heard of them for several months, and then like a bolt from the blue in walked the R.C.M.P. with a warrant, seized the books, and a prosecution was launched. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that reveals a very highhanded attitude. If foreign exchange control must continue then I put the responsibility on the Minister of Finance to see that this highhanded attitude ceases on the part of the officials concerned.
In saying that, I am not going to underestimate the size of the task they have to perform. If we are going to have foreign exchange control, then of course there must be administration, and there must be enforcement, but I think just as important as the letter of the law is the spirit that is instilled into the officials responsible for the administration and enforcement. In that respect it seems to me, with deference, that the Minister of Finance and the chairman of the board could have a beneficial influence.
There is one other matter. I am still concerned about the possibility of the use of this measure for the purpose of regulating or prohibiting in some way or other the movement of goods. I do not wish to thresh old straw. We recall the assurance given to the house on this subject by the Minister of Finance on June 17, 1946, when he said, at page 2547 of Hansard:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
On that assurance the bill went to the banking and commerce committee of the house. A good deal has been said about what occurred before the banking and commerce committee of the other place, but some things of importance transpired in the banking and commerce committee of this house. I wish to mention briefly two passages in the evidence given by Mr. Rasminsky to the banking and commerce committee of this house on July 15, 1946. At page 55 of the record this question was put to him:
There is one remark of Mr. Rasminsky's that I should like to ask a question about.
Then reference is made to it, and reference is made to sections 25, 26 and 27 of the act. Then this statement is made in the question:
Surely it is not a complete answer to say that protection is provided in what are apparently intended to be the saving or reassuring clauses, section 25, subsection 2, section 26, subsection 2, and section

27, subsection 3. They do not go so far as to remove from the foreign exchange control board all regulatory power with reference to the movement of goods, currency and securities.
Then follows Mr. Rasminsky's answer:
I do think that the subsections to which you have just referred very definitely have this effect, that they make it impossible for the board to withhold permits for the import or export of goods except on two grounds, one, that the payment is not in a currency which has been specified as the appropriate currency for that transaction; and two, on the ground that, there is an improper valuation placed on the transaction.
Mr. Rasminsky, the alternate chairman of the foreign exchange control board, said there were only two grounds on which freedom for the movement of goods could be refused under the provisions of the act. Again at page 57 there is this question:
In other words, the suggestion there is no regulatory power vested in the board with reference to imports at the expense of any power parliament now has in that regard, Mr. Rasminsky, was referring to the export and import of goods rather than securities and currency?
Mr. Rasminsky answered:
That is right.
We know what happened in November, 1947. This house is entitled to the assurance that the act is not going to be used again- or, more accurately, abused again-for a purpose that was specifically disclaimed by the Minister of Finance in introducing the measure, and by the alternate chairman of the board in giving his evidence in the passages to which I have referred. Before the bill is reported to the house I think the minister should be prepared to give assurance that, except in the two cases referred to by Mr. Rasminsky which are clearly within the terms of the act, the act will not be used again to restrict the movement of goods across the border.
It is unfortunate that there is not an opportunity provided now for a review of the whole administration of the act, and a review of the provisions of the act, as there was three years ago when the bill was before us. It is a great pity, because the provisions of this act ought to be very carefully scrutinized by the banking and commerce committee of the house in the light of nearly three years' experience under the terms of this statute. I think the banking and commerce committee would insist on a goodly number of amendments being made if the committee had the opportunity to make that review.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the minister should give the house some statement as to his objective. It is not good enough to go on saying, "We believe that a need exists for the continuation of the measure; we are not prepared to say when the act should come to an end, and we are asking in the meantime for a
Foreign Exchange Control two-year extension." We had statements of a similar nature when the bill was previously before the house, and I think the house ought to have a clear statement from the minister as to specifically what he is aiming at in that regard. His predecessor as Minister of Finance had this to say on June 17, 1946, in introducing the measure, at page 2547 of Hansard:
We hope-
He is speaking now of the character of the financial relations between nations.
-that it will be one which does not call for restrictive controls and we shall do everything in our power to bring this about.
Again on page 2547 of Hansard he said, following the passage I read earlier disclaiming any intention to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement:
We expect to be able to avoid any interference with current account transactions.
Will the minister give the house some statement as to what his objectives are? Surely the minister must be prepared to subscribe to freedom in this matter as the objective to which the house should be bending its efforts, to which the administration ought to be bending its efforts, and to which the whole purpose of the administration of this measure ought now to be directed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the latter part of my hon. friend's speech was directed rather more to the principles of the bill than to the details of the sections. I do not know that I can add very much to what I said in my rather lengthy speech last Thursday. As to what the government has in mind in asking for the continuation of this measure, in the disturbed condition in which we find ourselves today in the world I look on it as a sort of measure of national defence. I am firmly convinced that we need exchange control, and that we shall continue to need it for some little time yet; but as I have had occasion to say numerous other times when this legislation has been before the house, it is open to the government of the day or to parliament at any time to repeal this measure. It does not have to wait until it lapses by mere passage of time. There is not much, if anything, that I can add to what I said in my speech last Thursday as to the reasons why the government feels that it must ask for the continuation of this measure.
Will the minister give assurance against the use of the act to limit the movement of goods across international boundaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not going to give formal assurance as to anything. As the committee will recall, the foreign exchange control

Foreign Exchange Control order was used in November of 1947 to control the importation of goods into the country. As I stated frankly at that time, it had never been contemplated that power was contained in the act. In those circumstances I think it was very fortunate that it was there. Concurrently with the use of those powers we introduced into the house a specific bill which is now the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, in which we put in statutory form the prohibitions and quotas on the importation of goods. I can certainly say, however, that the government has no intention at this moment of using the Foreign Exchange Control Act in that way. The committee will recall that in the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act there is a specific provision that its prohibitions and quotas cannot be increased except by a statute of this house. We can relax, but we cannot increase the prohibitions; I think the law will have to speak for itself.

I intend to support this measure, but I should also like to express my support for the suggestion put forward by the member for Fraser Valley. I think it was a practical and reasonable suggestion. I also represent a border constituency in which there are a number of people who go back and forth to the United States. Under the present regulations the United States currency they have when they return to Canada is turned into the bank but is not credited to the $150 total United States funds they are allowed per year. If a person returns the unspent balance of this United States money to the bank, in my opinion it should be credited to the total of $150 a person is allowed. I ask the minister if it would be possible to change the regulations in this respect to give effect to that suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be very glad to discuss it with the board. I do not see why it should not be done, but there may be good reasons for not doing it. I will certainly explore the matter. I am sorry, but I cannot stay any longer this evening. If the committee is not ready to report the bill, I shall have to adjourn the debate.
Will the minister inform the house who this Mr. C. A. Rowe is, who was appointed-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have to get some information as to that. All I can say at the moment is that he is an employee of the board. I do not know what his particular duties are or from where he comes.
As long as the minister says he will inform the house-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will obtain the information and inform the house.

I think the minister should be allowed to leave, since he has an important engagement, and we can go on with something else.
Progress reported.
