speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 86, to amend the Continuation or Transitional Measures Act, 1947.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill, an act to amend the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, I should like to review and, if I can, to clarify some of the issues which have emerged in relation to it. Whatever he may think as to the continuance of the emergency up to the present time, no member will deny that during world war II a national emergency arose.
To deal with the problems created by this national emergency, the government introduced a number of economic and financial controls in respect to matters which it was admitted under normal peacetime conditions would fall within section 92 of the British North America Act and within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The government's authority to deal with these matters was not established by this parliament. It was established by the War Measures Act which was passed in 1914 to deal with a similar emergency created by world war I.
Section 2 of the War Measures Act, 1914, provides that the issue of a proclamation by His Majesty or under the authority of the governor in council shall be conclusive evidence that the war exists and of its continuance, until by the issue of a further proclamation it is declared that the war no longer exists. At the end of world war I the War Measures Act was not repealed and therefore, when world war II began, the government had only to proclaim on September 1, 1939, the War Measures Act of 1914 in order to eliminate all conflicts of jurisdiction between the provinces and dominion. This granted supremacy to the federal parliament to the extent that it was necessary to deal with the emergency of world war II.
Many harsh things have been said by our Progressive Conservative friends in this house concerning the orders in council now under

discussion and the alleged bureaucrats who administered them, including the alleged No.
1 and No. 2 bureaucrats, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). The leader of the opposition alleges that the present Liberal administration in connection with these orders in council has been guilty of centralization, dictatorial bureaucracy, and invasion of provincial rights, and I believe also of incipient totalitarianism.
Characteristically, he has not at any time taken the trouble to prove these serious charges. We of course emphatically deny them. Most of the orders in council complained about, which authorize all of this alleged bureaucracy, were passed under this War Measures Act of 1914, introduced by a Conservative government under the leadership of Sir Robert Borden and left on the statute books at the end of world war I by the Union government presided over by a Conservative. Order in council P.C. 8528, which is the key order, was drafted as a copy of an order passed during world war I under the War Measures Act, and the words, "unreasonable and unjust", stood the test of time from 1914 until they were somewhat disturbed by the decision in the McGinn case just a few weeks ago.
In saying this, sir, I am implying no criticism whatever of Sir Robert Borden or of the Conservative government in 1914. On the contrary, I say he was right in passing the War Measures Act and we have been right in invoking that act. It is the leader of the opposition and his colleagues in this house now who are wrong in criticizing us for invoking the act passed at that time.
At the end of world war II, the present government did not continue to act under the War Measures Act. As soon as the war ended, this government, which is now charged by the leader of the opposition with flouting the authority of parliament, came back to this parliament for authority for the transitional powers it required to carry on in the post-war years. This authority took the form of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, the preamble to which recites, among other things, the following:
And whereas the national emergency arising out of the war has continued since the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan and is still continuing;
And whereas it is essential in the national interest that certain transitional powers continue to be exercisable by the governor in council during the continuation of the exceptional conditions brought about by war-
Transitional Measures Act
This is a very pregnant statement-
-and it is preferable that such transitional powers be exercised hereafter under special authority in that behalf conferred by parliament instead of being exercised under the War Measures Act.
In other words, sir, the moment the war was over, instead of this government in any way disregarding the rights and powers of parliament, it ceased to invoke the War Measures Act and came back to parliament for authority to carry on during the post-war period. Thus when our Conservative friends rant in this house about restoring to parliament the powers of parliament, they completely ignore the fact that as soon as the war was over this Liberal government, true to its traditions of acknowledging at all times the' supremacy of parliament, came back to this house for the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, just as we now seek the passage of the bill which is now before the house. But what our friends of the Conservative party must not forget, I suggest with all deference, is that it is the majority of parliament which determines these matters and not the minority, no matter how noisy and truculent it may be.
After 1945, having secured the authority to carry on in the post-war period, this government came back in 1946 to call for an amendment to the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act of 1945. Then, in the further development of this policy of consulting parliament at all times for authority for each new phase of decontrol, in 1947 this government came back to parliament seeking the passage of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947. To this act at that time was attached a schedule which, as it was originally presented-as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) said the other day-contained fifty-seven orders in council; but those had been whittled down to fifty before the bill got through the house. These orders in council -that is, the exact text of the orders in council themselves-were laid before the house in their entirety. Then, order by order and section by section, they were gone over by this parliament; and they will appear in the schedule to that act, with the amendments which were made by parliament to those orders in council indicated as part of the schedule. In other words, parliament approved these orders in precisely the same way that it would approve the sections of a statute. Any suggestion that the procedure followed was a secret procedure or a flouting of parliament is not in any way supported by the facts. More than that, by section 4 of this 1947 act, it was provided that in addition to these orders in council
1728

Transitional Measures Act set out in the schedule to this act of 1947- the terms of which orders in council had been approved of by parliament-the governor in council might revoke in whole or in part any order or regulation, but he could not amend any order or regulation. That means that far from parliament having delegated-as it has done on a number of occasions and as it is quite proper for parliament to do-legislative power to the governor in council, parliament in that bill did no such thing. It undertook itself to go over the exact terms of the orders in council; and by the terms of the act which this government introduced the governor in council was limited to the revocation of the orders but had no authority to amend them in any way.
Was this procedure a flouting of parliamentary authority? Did the consultation of parliament, year by year, take away from parliament's powers? Did the prohibition under section 4, which prevented the governor in council from amending the orders in council which parliament had approved and placed in the schedule to this act, give unto the governor in council any dictatorial, bureaucratic powers, as those words are used by the leader of the opposition? Did the duration of the act until not later than March 31, 1948, as provided in section 7 of that act-thus necessitating the government's coming back to parliament within approximately one year -indicate upon the part of this government a desire to destroy or prejudice parliamentary authority? Surely, Mr. Speaker, the answer to each of these questions is a resounding no.

speechtext:
"Chubby Power" would be about as good an answer as my hon. friend could give to that question. Chubby Power is the answer. That is the only power that was not exercised. Certainly parliament did not fail to exercise legislative powers. In 1947, as I am informed, and as the leader of the opposition seems not to have been informed, this parliament went over not only the sections of the act but the provisions of the orders in council with more care than it takes with the average statute. As I have pointed out, having done so it prohibited the governor in council from amending these orders in council in any way. Although it is a commonplace thing for parliament to delegate to the governor in council legislative powers, the government on this occasion did not ask for that delegation and it was not granted. The orders in council were passed by parliament and they stayed as parliament had passed them, and were so administered and enforced.
Parliament delegated to the executive nothing but executive powers. Is it, perchance, the executive power that our hon. friends of the Conservative opposition want restored to parliament? If so, surely they have enough experience in public life to know that it is nonsense to suggest that parliament hires the administrators, accountants, and clerks to administer this law. Far from having ignored parliament, this government has gone back to parliament every year and not only has submitted to it, but the government itself has suggested, these limitations upon its own authority.
This, sir, is by no means all that this government has done to respect parliamentary authority and to accomplish orderly control.
From 1947 onward the government in its requests to parliament voluntarily has limited itself to the continuation of orders in council which parliament has seen and approved. From 1947 on, the government has been

deprived of any rights there might have been under the War Measures Act to pass any orders in council to deal with any other subject matters. Under the provisions of this War Measures Act, put on the statute books by the Borden administration, all that the government had to do was to carry on and invoke its powers in almost any direction. As soon as the war was over it came to this parliament and limited itself voluntarily to powers actually delegated by this parliament.
From 1947 until the present time this government has revoked thirty-eight of the fifty orders in council that appear in the schedule to the 1947 act. More than that, the ministers of this government have stated time and time again that the remaining controls will be lifted at the earliest time that it is safe to do so. In connection with at least one of these controls, namely, rent controls, a sincere effort was made in good faith to get the provincial governments, some of whom had been very jealous of their provincial rights, to exercise their provincial rights in relation to the subject of rent control. But strangely enough, when it came to doing something rather than merely talking about provincial rights, there was not the same amount of zeal about the exercise of them.

speechtext: I suggest, sir, that such a worry, such a perturbation upon the part of the leader of the opposition within minutes after the vote had been cast, betokens a rather troubled conscience. Methinks, Mr. Speaker, the lady doth protest too much.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He is no lady.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And, sir, my hon. friend's protests impress, and I suggest that his threats frighten, no one. He has used this short and descriptive word with regard to so many honourable, decent and often distinguished citizens, that it is almost a mark of distinction for him to admit others to their company. It is getting to be that no man in public life today can really claim to have arrived unless he has been called names by the hon. gentleman. It is like a picture by Karsh in reverse. The Karsh picture flatters, and the harsh names of my hon. friend offend, but they are both, with apologies to Mr. Karsh, the hallmarks of arrival.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What section of the bill is the minister speaking on now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I shall be very glad to answer my hon. friend. I am speaking on the statement of his leader that he would apply a short and descriptive word to any person who commented upon the vote that was cast by my hon. friend's party on this bill.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What has Karsh got to do with that?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister had his picture taken by Karsh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend the other day issued an invitation to the members of this house. He invited us to listen so that we might learn something about constitutional matters in Canada by no more complicated a device than listening to him.
Well, sir, I must say that for a man who professes to be such an expert in this field he portrays, in my opinion, on every occasion on which he speaks concerning it, a most superficial grasp of the principles involved. And as compared with those of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), for example, or the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), or the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), his legal arguments upon it neither merit nor warrant a reply. His statements do not make sense even as to the facts. He says, for example, that if there be such an emergency as we allege, then that emergency could be invoked for the purpose of a wholesale invasion of provincial rights.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
And the hon. member says "hear, hear." What are the facts? With these powers which he says we have taken unto ourselves, what have we done? Over a period of years, since the Transitional Measures Act was passed in 1947, and even before that, we have followed a policy of continuous and orderly decontrol practised by this government, which is the very antithesis of any invasion of provincial rights. So that any suggestion such as the one that has been made, that this general emergency which we invoke as the basis for our law, is going to be seized upon for a wholesale invasion of provincial rights, is quite without foundation.
Even the very control which he says he is in favour of, namely rental control, has not been continued by this government until sincere attempts had been made to have the provinces take over this field, if they were prepared to do so. Does this look like an invasion of provincial rights? Does it support any of the extravagant language and the extravagant charges and accusations which my hon. friend has been making so freely at every stage of the debate on this bill? Certainly not.
He drags in, as he has dragged in on every possible occasion, whether it was relevant or not, the old chestnut which is just as incorrect this time as on every other occasion on which he has repeated it, to the effect that after the war the dominion government did not return to the provinces their taxing

powers. This, sir, I suggest is a statement and argument which is intended for consumption by the uninformed; because no one else would pay any attention to it. The constitution, of which my hon. friends are the stout defenders, gave to the dominion government from the very beginning, in 1867, completely unlimited taxing powers. The dominion government does not have to ask any provincial consent to impose any form of taxation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What section is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I tell my hon. friend that I am replying to the argument which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) considered so relevant to this matter, which he introduced in the house, and which hon. members and Mr. Speaker permitted him to speak upon, and to which they listened.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are both out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If that could be done, then surely we are at liberty to correct a record which has been left in the state in which he left it.
The facts are that during the war the dominion purchased from the provinces exclusive powers in the fields of income and corporation taxes by paying to the provinces good and valuable consideration fixed in freely negotiated agreements between the provinces and the dominion. During the period of the agreement the Drew government in Ontario accumulated an aggregate surplus on current account of over $46,800,000.
At the expiration of this agreement the provinces were offered a generous substitute for it, which substitute recognized and affirmed the provinces' constitutional rights to impose all these taxes if they chose to do so. Again, the provinces were free to accept or not to accept. Two of them, Ontario and Quebec, in point of fact did not accept. The wartime tax suspension agreements had been complied with to the letter, and any statement that the dominion failed to return to the provinces their taxing powers, Mr. Speaker, is just not true.
My hon. friend and members of his party are quite within their rights in a free country and in a free parliament to get up in their places and say that it was his-
-declared desire that the dominion-provincial conference of 1945-46 should succeed.
And in this he is precisely correct. It was his "declared" desire. The record is larded with pious statements to this effect. And he is hlso quite within his rights in the closing hours of the conference to demand as the
Transitional Measures Act price of its success $50 million more than all the provincial revenues, including dominion subsidies, before the war.
My hon. friend is quite entitled in a free country to say that he is entirely in favour of Newfoundland entering Canada; and his party, as he claims, in order to save the Canadian constitution, is entirely at liberty to vote against Newfoundland entering Canada.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order, order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He is entirely free in this issue-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. Surely this is not only irrelevant but it is miles and miles from anything connected with the bill we are talking about at the present time-as is 90 per cent of what the minister has said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In some respects I quite agree with the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). But I am replying to the arguments made by his leader in this debate, and the hon. member for Calgary West should have been more assiduous when the subjects were first introduced in calling the house to order.
As I was saying when I was interrupted by my hon. friend-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I want a ruling on my point of order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order. I am listening to the minister. If I thought he was out of order it would be my duty to intervene, and I would intervene.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I say that it is-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are in order. Mr. Speaker said so. Everything is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition is entirely free in this issue now before us to say that he and his party favour rent control, and he is entirely free to vote against the resolution which would continue it.
But, sir, I think he will find as time goes on, before he gets finished with these manoeuvres, that the Canadian citizens are too intelligent to be taken in by these conflicts between his words and his deeds.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Give them a chance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
And, this being a free country, they will not be deterred from saying what they think about it by any threats about the use of a short and descriptive word. They will be more disposed to consider his opposition in the light of the fact that the authority which this government has exercised under the War Measures Act of the Borden government has been exercised at all times with a

Transitional Measures Act scrupulous regard for the rights and privileges of parliament.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that is not true. Thank goodness in a free parliament he will have the opportunity shortly to get up and prove that it is not true, if he can.
Immediately after the fall of Japan this country went to parliament and secured the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, which has been subject ever since to annual review by parliament.
As I have pointed out, not only has parliament determined the text of the orders in council under which the governor in council has acted since 1947, but the government in acting under those orders in council has carried on an orderly, and latterly an accelerated, decontrol which is still continuing. This government is committed to decontrol, even in respect of the residual controls that are being maintained, as soon as it is safe to do so.
Finally, the fact that two of the opposition parties in this house have supported this bill in its different stages is eloquent tribute to the rightness of the government's action in asking parliament to pass it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate and I would not have done so except for the splendid schoolboy essay just read by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson).

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: His master's voice.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would like to hear you all, so I would ask you to speak one at a time. That would be much better. I do want to compliment the minister upon the splendid reading he has just given us. I intend to deal with just two or three things, and I shall deal with the major one first.
The minister has told us that this government has been so generous and kind to us in the opposition and so careful of the interests of the people of the country that they brought this thing back year after year in order to get parliament's support. Of course the answer to that is that the legislation within itself contains the provision that it is only for one year. Therefore they had to come back under the legislation and not through the great kindness that lies in the hearts of members of the cabinet. In fact, in times gone by, it was urged that it should be passed as it was only for a year, that at the end of that time it would probably die a natural death. That takes care of that part.
IMr. Garson.]

Then the minister says that they have eliminated these various things. I ask this simple question even of my impatient brethren across the road, and I assure them that I will not be very long: After the government control over steel, lumber and farm products, what is there left? That takes in the total economy of this country. It may be that there are other industries, other efforts and other energies expended in dealing with other things, but without those three your economy stops dead. A year or so ago we learned that you do not need a general strike in Canada to stop our economy, that all that was needed was a strike in a basic industry.
Dealing now with this matter of rent control, short words and that sort of thing, I suppose the minister was referring to what we usually term as being short, ugly four-letter words or something of that kind. What does it amount to? On the occasion when there were fifty-seven varieties it was put up to this parliament, as it is put up now with the twelve varieties, that we must accept the whole package or go without. We on this side do not and will not accept that sort of judgment. We will not compromise with ourselves or with our people and say that because A, B and C are good, D, E, F, G and so on are bad; that we are going to compromise and vote for all things because there are two or three good ones wrapped up in the package. That is exactly the position that we are taking at the present time and in so far as I know will continue to take as long as we are here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Could the hon. member inform the house what the bad things are?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I shall answer the minister's question and deal immediately with two of the things which are bad. I shall read from the orders in council dealing with steel and lumber and then I shall ask the minister if in his judgment and wide experience he thinks that the government needs the powers given in those orders in order to carry out the things the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has in his mind. I think that is- a fair suggestion. I brought down these books thinking that we might be in committee, when I intended to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce about this. But since we have this volunteer across the road perhaps I might mention them to him.
I am reading from the statutory orders and regulations, volume 1, 1946, beginning at page 131. I do not want to read all the order in council, but later on I shall read from page 133. Paragraph (c) reads:
To enter on, take possession of, and utilize any mine, land, plant, factory, mill, refinery, smelter,

foundry, warehouse, building, or place or any equipment used or capable of being used for the purpose of producing or dealing in or with steel and to deal in or with or take possession of any vehicles, cars, ships, locomotives, or other equipment deemed by the steel controller to be required or useful for the operation of any such mine, plant, factory, mill, refinery, smelter, foundry, warehouse, building, or place and/or for producing or dealing in or with steel or equipment; provided that any order of the steel controller made under the powers vested in him by this paragraph (c) shall be subject to any conflicting valid order of the transport controller appointed by the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport.
That is only one paragraph of about twenty. Then the definition of "dealing in or with" is given in paragraph (d), which reads:
"dealing in or with" shall include buying, selling, leasing, hiring, exchanging, acquiring, importing, exporting, storing, supplying, delivering, operating, transporting, distributing, shipping, conveying, installing, allocating, consuming or using and "deal in or with" and "dealt in or with" shall have corresponding and similarly extended meanings.
I will not read the definition of steel, but it covers everything that has any ferrous metal in it. My recollection is that ferrous means "pertaining to or derived from iron", so it would mean anything with a component part containing some iron. Under this the government could go and take a farmer's tractor away from him if it was thought it were needed in some little business engaged in dealing in or with steel. There are many more paragraphs. I am going to stop and ask the minister now whether he thinks that, with regard to the present emergency as to steel, the government needs the powers I have read in that one paragraph. Does he think so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have no hesitation whatever in saying that I think none of my hon. friend's remarks are substantially relevant to the matter under discussion.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They are not substantially relevant to the matter under discussion, and when I close the debate I will take the occasion to deal with them.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are running out on him.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I thank the minister for his great generosity in telling me that he will put his boys to work and probably find an answer to what I have said, and that he will let me know what the answer is when that time arrives. May I say that under that order there is a steel controller, an associate steel controller, a deputy steel controller, all of whom may depute other persons who may do all of these things. Discretion is completely given to these individuals to do all the things that the controller himself is entitled to do, and the only appeal is to the controller himself. Then
Transitional Measures Act again all these individuals have the most complete protection from actions, and so on; no matter how wrongful their acts may be they have complete protection under this statute. When the minister is boning up on his reply I wonder if he would include that part of it in the answer he is going to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do so.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Then I will say a word or two about lumber. I think the difference between lumber and steel is that there is no associate controller. There is only a timber controller and a deputy controller. I said that I was not going to be long, and I mean that. Therefore, without going into all the various regulations, and under one paragraph they run from "a" to "s", I think it fair to say as to the lumber situation-and I hope you will correct me if I am wrong- that the powers are practically the same as those with respect to steel.
Why have I put that forward, Mr. Speaker? Because it seems to me that we have argued, and I think validly argued, that if there be an emergency requiring certain things these matters should be dealt with differently. As I understood it, the explanation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had to do largely with priorities, and had to do largely with saying that we need this type of manufactured steel rather than that. I think I am correctly stating what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said. Therefore I come back to what the Minister of Justice said, which was that they brought this emergency business, these controls by order in council, before parliament each year, and I say to him, Why has he not studied these various controls to eliminate from the orders in council to which I have just referred the powers that they do not need to take care of present needs, even accepting their word for what those needs are?
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that in this same bill we have controls on certain products of agriculture. I mean prices of agricultural products. Let me repeat for the last time tonight, and if I have the strength I will continue to do so, that we are prepared to consider, to receive, and to support certain controls, rent control if you like, if it is brought to us as a bill, as a statute or as an order in council where the rights of landlord and tenant are clearly set out, and which is not subject to change every few weeks as rent control has been. Then we will support it with a good heart. But we will not under any circumstances, and I hope we never shall, take a great large package of twelve things running from butter through timber to steel, and support that or get nothing. As far as I am concerned, I intend to oppose the measure, and I have no hesitation in doing so-

Transitional Measures Act
Is it laziness? Is it inattention? What is it? The minister said a moment ago that this decontrol was progressive. Let it progress to the place where we may deal with those essential items in our economy one at a time. Let us find out the necessity in the particular case and vote on it accordingly, rather than have this grab box handed to us with a game of bingo to support it, because that is about the only reason that has been given by the minister up to this time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh yes, indeed, but do not make it too long.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: During the eight years in which these two orders in council have been in force has he ever heard anyone complain about the injustice of their operation?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh yes, many, many times.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can he give me one instance?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can give you many. May I congratulate the minister and say to him that he does not overstep the mark and does not intend to. But many of his officials who are enforcing these regulations do so.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are quite mistaken about the latter.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I listened tonight with a great deal of interest to the minister and to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I think first of all, if I may say so, that the member for Calgary West, with his usual eloquence, was flogging a very dead horse. The bill before us today is a vital one, because it brings parliament face to face once again with what is probably Canada's thorniest domestic problem. As we begin this debate I think there are two significant facts which have developed. I think this may be remembered as a historical night. It will be remembered as such a night because, when the bill is passed, it means that Canada has virtually come to the end of the road as far as controls are concerned. We have been led down the last lap of the route leading to complete decontrol. This night will go down in the history of Canada secondly because George Drew, the hon. member for Carleton, has won his first major political victory, in making the government prematurely throw out all these controls.
The insidious-I do not know whether that word is parliamentary-pressure of the Conservative party has culminated tonight in forcing the government to sacrifice the interests of the average Canadian to the interests

of a few privileged citizens. Those are the two significant points in this debate so far.
I hope that hon. members, even on the government side, will yet consider the matter very carefully before they pass the bill because I think they should keep in mind that in the last three and a half years the cost of living index has gone up forty points.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What about wages?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am talking about the cost of living index. I will come to wages in a moment. On August 1, 1945, the cost of living index stood at 119-6, and today, with pretty well all controls removed, it stands at 159-4. I am not going to go again over all that has been said on the resolution. All I want to say with increased emphasis is that the average Canadian has been hurt by decontrol, particularly those in the low-wage income groups, and more particularly pensioners. I think that the inflation I have mentioned indicates, beyond any reasonable doubt, to any reasonable man that parliament so far has failed to deal effectively with the cost of living problem. For a number of years the government has been content to drift along, to hope that something will turn up, to hope that prices will go down of their own volition. I think ultimately prices will come down, but in the meantime a great many people will have been hurt, and hurt unnecessarily. This very stubborn government attitude has benefited primarily only one segment of Canadian society and that is the business and commercial interests.
The other night the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out that, in the period between 1945 and 1947, profits after taxes of 655 of Canada's largest corporations went up 64 per cent, while in the same period the cash income from farm produce went up only 17 per cent. The member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) asked me about wages a moment ago, and I should like to tell him about wages. For instance, in the iron and steel industry-I am sorry I cannot tell him about the lumber industry-weekly wages rose in the period I have mentioned about 9 per cent while profits for that industry rose 66 per cent; in the pulp and paper industry wages went up 23 per cent but profits only 247 per cent. One could give other examples. In almost every case, profits rose much more rapidly than wages.
By means of Bill 86, which is before us tonight, the government is asking parliament for authority to continue certain controls and regulations for a limited period. I suppose we must take it that this is the government's 1949 answer to the cost of living problem. I remember that a year ago this

house was discussing the same problem and had before it a bill of a somewhat similar nature. I remember that even at that time the cost of living was causing concern throughout the country. Every hon. member will recall having received thousands of petitions from protesting citizens, labour unions and the like. All members will also recollect that, about a year ago, the Institute of Public Opinion conducted a poll, which revealed that the majority of Canadians desired the reimposition of some controls.
When Bill 136 was introduced a year ago, those were the circumstances. That bill was quite different from this bill, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) pointed out. The bill of a year ago gave parliament the power to reimpose controls over the whole broad field if it deemed it necessary. I think it would be fair to say that most hon. members expected, when they gave the government those very wide and comprehensive powers a year ago, that the government would use them to fight inflation. I recall the member for Bonaventure, I think it was, a government supporter, speaking in the debate. He said that drastic measures should be taken immediately in order to bring the cost of living index back to where it was in 1946. He said we could not rely upon time and laissez faire to solve this problem, and price ceilings should be reimposed immediately on timber and basic commodities. A Liberal member said that. I believe there was an indication a year ago that parliament and the country expected the government to use the powers it was given in Bill 136. The country expected some action from the government. But in the past twelve months the government has stubbornly refused to do anything about reimposing controls where it was necessary.
On the contrary, while still piously professing to follow a policy of orderly decontrol, the government has been removing subsidies and controls just as rapidly as they dared in the face of public opinion. Hundreds of controls have been eliminated in the past year and there are almost no subsidies left. In other words, instead of using the powers given in Bill 136 a year ago, the government has practically scuttled the whole system of controls and subsidies. The result, of course, has been a very substantial increase in the cost of living.
Rather than take any tangible action as they were empowered to do, to reimpose controls, in February, 1948, the government set up a parliamentary prices committee. The C.C.F. attitude towards that committee was very clearly expressed by the member for
Transitional Measures Act Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) at page 761 of Hansard, when he said:
. . . we are of the opinion that, in the present crisis in Canada, the people demand not the establishment of a parliamentary committee, but rather some effective step to meet the situation.
When the government refused to take specific action, we did participate in the committee. We did our best to make that committee a reasonable success. Some of our members spent a good many hours on that committee. We knew in advance that the committee could not possibly succeed in lowering prices because its powers were so limited. The only power that the prices committee had was the power to talk. Even if it found acts which were anti-social, there was nothing it could do about them. Thus while the committee sat, prices continued to rise. The members of the committee sat back impotent and helpless; we were restrained from any concrete action by our limited terms of reference.
However, I am not going to say much more about the prices committee except that after sitting for months, and after having heard mountains of evidence, a report was finally brought down in this house. I think it would be fair to say that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and his government supporters brought down those recommendations. We who were in opposition could agree or disagree with them as we saw fit, but they were brought down by the minister. I suppose those recommendations were made in the belief that, if the government implemented them, perhaps something could be done to bring down the cost of living.
I think that was about nine months ago. If the government was sincere about wanting to do something to get prices down, surely ample time has elapsed.
I am not going to be very long, but I suggest we look at some of the recommendations of the prices committee for a moment. Recommendation one urged the setting up of a special commission to continue the work of the parliamentary committee. Before I pass along, I might say that that commission is still sitting. I understood it had finished its work before parliament opened this session, but it is still meeting, and I suppose the members are together drawing $100 or $200 per day of the taxpayers' money. The bills of the second session of 1945. That bill, Mr. Speaker, contained the mentality of the government with reference to the powers that it sought to take from parliament in 1945. The hue and cry was such in this house and elsewhere that it found its place into the deliberations of the dominion-provincial conference then in session. It may have escaped the recollection of the hon. gentleman, but the premiers of the provinces then assembled made it quite clear to the Prime Minister of that time that they would not consent, that they would not continue to deliberate with the federal government, if the federal government, by a measure of that kind, was going to trample underfoot the constitution of this country and usurp powers, not only powers which belonged to parliament, but powers which are reposed by the constitution of this country in the legislatures of the provinces. It was under a stream of protest, Mr. Speaker, that the government had to yield and withdraw that iniquitous Bill 15.
Such was the mind of this government, Mr. Speaker, that they were determined to usurp everything that they could, and with a submissive majority in this house they were able to take from parliament in a bill which did become law, and is chapter 25 of the statutes of the second session of 1945, the following powers as enumerated in section 2, which reads as follows:
2. (1) The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may, by reason of the continued existence of the national emergency arising out of the war against Germany and Japan, deem necessary or advisable for the purpose of . . .
Then there is a series, and (c) reads thus:
(c) maintaining, controlling and regulating supplies and services, prices, transportation, use and occupation of property, rentals, employment, salaries and wages to ensure economic stability and an orderly transition to conditions of peace.
This government wanted absolute power, Mr. Speaker. It wanted all the powers that are reposed in parliament, and it wanted all the powers that are reposed by the constitution in the legislatures of the provinces. That is what this government wanted, and that is the shameful record that the Minister of Justice has the effrontery to stand up in this house tonight and defend, when he says to this house that the moment the war was over this government ceased to act under the War Measures Act, and that it came forward and

did things in a statutory way. What did it do, Mr. Speaker? It took from parliament powers that no government that has any sense of responsibility to the constitution or to the people has any right to demand in time of peace.

We like these orders in council. We have been operating under them, and we have our boards and commissions set up to operate under them. We do not like to make any change. I wish to put him right on one other thing. He says that if the resolution preceding this bill had not passed on Friday night we would not have rent control. It would mean that the government would have an opportunity and that the government would have a duty to introduce a proper measure to bring about a continuation of rent control, and to do it in proper legislative form, and in a form which would recognize the responsibility of the government to parliament.
There has been so much misrepresentation on the subject of the position of this party with respect to the emergency and rent control that I should like briefly to say one or two things on the subject. One finds in the bill today no reference whatever to a national emergency. If the government is so convinced that there is today what the Minister
[Mr. Fleming.)

of Justice contended in his speech on Friday last, namely, a general emergency, a general national emergency-and note the word "general"-then one would have thought that the government would have invited the house to make a clear declaration on the point, or that at the very least there would be in the bill a recital of the continuance of the national emergency. But, no; the Minister of Justice does not like to bring that subject too directly before the House of Commons. So he simply relies upon a continuance of the recital in the preamble to the 1947 bill. That is as close as he wants to bring this subject before the house, and into the discussion on the bill.
My leader made it perfectly clear, and the house can see it at pages 1446 and 1448 of Hansard, that this Progressive Conservative party did not oppose rent control. The Progressive Conservative leader and those associated with him say that we are quite prepared and ready to support a proper measure of rent control. But we do not wish to see it done in this form. We wish to see it done in proper legislative form. And that is the position every member in the House of Commons ought to take, if he has any respect for his responsibility as a member of the House of Commons.

speechtext: So you are for controls, eh? Running back and forth.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We are for controls, but in proper form-not the kind of form to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has been so long accustomed-a man who, however sound his mind may have been when he entered parliament, has wielded such extraordinary powers for so long that one can see in him the truth of the famous statement of Lord Acton that all power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
Mr. Speaker, the house must make up its mind whether it proposes to proceed by a proper legislative and responsible method, such as we have advocated, or by this omnibus holus-bolus method the government is asking parliament to accept.
Bear this in mind, that we of the Progressive Conservative party have shown how the matter of rent control can be handled. We have shown how it ought to be handled in this House of Commons by proper methods, by a proper legislative enactment which would be clear and which would give to members of the house an opportunity to do their duty, a duty they owe to their constituents, the duty of carefully reviewing legislation before it becomes law. This is impossible to do in connection with these orders in council.
There are some members in the house who have not very much patience with a

discussion about the constitution. That is the kind of mentality that is found in hon. members as a result of the doubtful example set by the government opposite. I wish to give ample warning to those who are prepared to heed warnings that the course that is being followed, in regard to this measure in its present form, is one which may well lead to a defeat of the whole scheme of rent control and of other controls, if this bill should be challenged in the courts.
We have given the House of Commons a clear statement as to how this matter could be handled without jeopardizing the whole system of controls, including rent controls, if the House of Commons would follow the legislative methods we propose.
The Minister of Justice has made it perfectly clear that in his judgment-and in this respect he is correct; that is the one place in his speech where he was right-there is no power in the subjects enumerated in section 91 of the British North America Act to legislate with reference to the matters dealt with in the twelve orders in council which are to be continued.
The minister justified the legislation on the strength of the existence of a general national emergency-not a specific emergency, but a general one. Let me say to the house, and to those who are not interested in the verities of the constitution, and who are not interested in warnings about what may be the fate of democracy if this house does not rise to its responsibilities, that they are jeopardizing everything in these orders in council today by their acceptance of the course the government is pursuing. They are jeopardizing everything.
If the government will bring in individual measures, as it ought to do, it may save the controls believed by the House of Commons to be necessary. But if this measure goes to the courts-this omnibus measure dealing with twelve orders in council on a wide variety of subjects-and if the courts are not satisfied that a national emergency exists with respect to each of these subjects, let us bear in mind the fact that the courts will not sit down and say, "Well, we will recognize the validity of the measure with respect to this control, but not with respect to that control or the other control". The courts are not going to sit down and separate the wheat from the chaff, separate what is ultra vires from what is intra vires.
May I remind the house of what the privy council did in 1937 when they had before them a reference with respect to the validity of the Employment and Social Insurance Act, 1935. The government asked the courts on
Transitional Measures Act that occasion to say whether that act or any part of it was within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada. They expressly asked the courts in case they found the whole measure was not intra vires of parliament to say what parts of it were. The reasons of the privy council will be found in 1937 Appeal Cases, page 355. In effect they said that they were not going to sit down to try to sift out the wheat from the chaff. Here is the concluding paragraph of the privy council's decision:
The other parts oi the act are so Inextricably mixed up with the insurance provisions of part III that it is impossible to sever them. It seems obvious, also, that in its truncated form, apart from part III, the act would never have come into existence. It follows that the whole act must be pronounced ultra vires.
The privy council were there dealing with only one statute and they were not prepared to say that part III might be intra vires while the rest of the act might be ultra vires. They said that they would not sit down and try to separate the parts that were intra vires from those that were ultra vires. Today we have a measure which cannot be compared as to clarity and specific directness with the statute under review in 1937; here we have an omnibus measure that simply scoops up the twelve remaining orders in council and says that they shall be law for another year. If this measure should go before the courts and it should be found that any part of it is ultra vires by reason of the general national emergency referred to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) not extending to that particular aspect of it, you may be sure that the whole bill will be ruled ultra vires. Think what a calamity there would be if the whole measure should be thrown out at a time when perhaps parliament was not in session. Would it not be the part of wisdom and common sense to divide up these various subjects and treat them individually, as they ought to be treated, and pass the proper legislative enactments with respect to each? That humble warning may fall on deaf ears, but if this measure is ruled ultra vires those words are on the record.
I wish to comment upon the proposition propounded in this house by the Minister of Justice in support of what he has had to say about the existence of no specific national emergency, if you please, but a general national emergency. He has put the validity of this measure on the basis of the existence of a general national emergency. The word "general" is his. If that general national emergency exists, as contended by the spokesman for the government, it is crystal clear that whether parliament occupies any field of legislative jurisdiction throughout the

Transitional Measures Act whole ambit of self-government in this country is simply a question of expediency or choice on the part of the government. So far as the constitutional argument is concerned, it goes this far: there is no field of legislative jurisdiction in Canada today into which this parliament may not enter by reason of the alleged existence of a general national emergency.

Slot machine is right. There is a great multitude of slot machines turning out the law, and this parliament is being asked to become a mere rubber stamp to give parliamentary authority to all kinds of order in council and regulation procedure.
We are told of amendments, but how on earth are we going to amend the orders in council when they do not appear before us in the text of this bill or in any statute of this parliament?
I am not going to go into the subject of surplus powers at any great length, but the twelve orders we are being asked to continue are just filled with powers that cannot by any possible stretch of the imagination be said to be necessary. Let any member of the government stand up and try to defend the necessity for the continuance of some of these orders in council. I will not go over the ground covered by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), but I just ask in passing if any hon. member of this house will stand up in his place and say, having regard to what may be suggested by hon. members opposite to be a national emergency, that it is essential in order to meet that national emergency that the priorities officer shall have power to prohibit the making of or dealing in construction materials, because that is what order in council P.C. 1609 says. It provides that the priorities officer shall have power to prohibit as well as to control and regulate the making of or dealing in construction materials. That is not an isolated

case; that is an example, and examples of the same kind can be multiplied by the score in these orders, containing as they do surplus and unnecessary powers that cannot be justified by the existence of anything that has been said at any time in this debate in relation to the alleged national emergency.
By continuing these powers in their present form this bill projects forward for another year the vice of delegation of power, the continuation of irresponsibility. Surely this House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, is not going to turn its back upon its clear responsibility in the matter.
It would be interesting to hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) what he, as premier of one of the provinces, had to say in 1945 when Bill 15 first came to the attention of the provincial premiers. Did he say, "Oh, you can trust this government with all power. Let us go right ahead. The war is over, but we will trust this government." Did he say that? If that was the position he took as a provincial premier in the fall of 1945 when the premiers of the provinces were meeting in conference in Ottawa, I would invite the Minister of Justice to stand up and say that he approved that bill. If, on the other hand, like the premiers of the other provinces, in obedience to their responsibility to the constitution, and to the people of their provinces, he stood up and protested, as did the premiers of the other provinces, against this highhanded, arbitrary usurpation of the powers of parliament and of the provinces, and joined them in protest, I think the house would like to know, because the house would like to have the opportunity of testing the glowing words that fell from the lips of the hon. gentleman tonight in relation to the stand he took with reference to that iniquitous Bill 15.
Would it not be comforting at least if the house and the people of the country had some assurance that the government was taking energetic measures to eliminate and to cure the conditions which constitute the national emergency that has been referred to? Would it not be comforting to know that they have some objective for meeting the critical national emergency that exists as to housing, and which justifies and makes necessary a proper measure of rent control today? Would that not have been of some comfort to the house in continuing these broad powers? Would it not have been of some comfort to the house on the other branch of the argument of the Minister of Justice? You will remember he said he supported his argument as to the national emergency on two grounds, first the housing emergency, which everybody on this side of the house knows more about than the government, and secondly, inflation? Would it not have been comforting if the
Transitional Measures Act minister had been able to tell us that the government was doing something to cure inflation, that this inflationary spiral, with which apparently they have been powerless to cope in recent years, was going to be cured by sensible government measures, and that the people of the country were going to be given an opportunity to meet the rising spiral of inflation, the rising cost of living, by reductions in income tax, by reductions in the burden of indirect taxes, all those consumer taxes that have weighed so oppressively upon the backs of the Canadian people?
My time is almost up, but before I conclude my remarks I wish to put forward an amendment which will give the house the opportunity that the government has not seen fit to give it, namely, to proceed with regard to this subject of rent control, and the other subject matters referred to in these twelve orders, by a proper legislative method. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon):
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to recommend a specific measure relating to rent control, and other specific measures relating respectively to other matters provided for in the said bill.
This amendment will give the house an opportunity to break down the measure. It will go to a committee; it will not now be read a second time. It will go to the banking and commerce committee, and the committee will have the opportunity of breaking down the subject matters that are dealt with today in the twelve orders in council. The committee will be able to bring in a proper specific measure with respect to rent control, a proper specific measure with regard to each of the other several matters dealt with in the twelve orders in council that are now under debate. That, Mr. Speaker, is a healthy and sensible procedure. It is the procedure that was followed in the house in 1946 when the government brought in a measure of a similar nature. It is true there was only one order in council involved, but it was a measure-

Let it not be said that there is not time to deal with it. The banking and commerce committee can be called together to meet at once. If it be said that there is not now time to deal with the matter adequately, if the government has left the banking and commerce committee too little time to deal with it properly, then we are quite prepared to have a short interim extension to give the banking and commerce committee time to do what this government has not given parliament time to do, to deal with this matter in a responsible way.
